items.title: The Edge of California Is Falling Into the Ocean
items.description: This season, El Niño is offering a glimpse of what the future has in store for California. Engorged with warm water, its waves powered by a frenzy of hurricanes, the Pacific Ocean has been clawing away huge chunks of the coast. Waves overtopped defensive sand berms and tore up the boardwalk on the Long Beach Peninsula, in Los Angeles County. Beaches in places such as Carlsbad, to the south, got wiped clean of sand. Train service to San Diego was interrupted. In Malibu, an access road to Point Dume, a promontory popular with hikers and surfers, partially collapsed from erosion. And on Labor Day weekend, in the driveway of Nicolas Cage’s beachfront home, a small sinkhole opened up. Francois Navarre, who once ran a paparazzi agency, had moved into the Malibu neighborhood just a few weeks before and discovered the hole while strolling down Sea Level Drive, the private street that runs behind a row of $8 million–to–$10 million homes, perched on pilings, that have an unimpeded view of the Pacific. The Palisades Fire had damaged Navarre’s home in Los Angeles last year, so he’d been living in Colorado. Now he could peer down through the pavement of his new neighborhood to the seawater coursing more than 20 feet below. The hole grew fast, expanding more every hour, Navarre told me. Gas and water lines soon ruptured. The ocean dislodged the home’s septic tank, which slammed into a neighbor’s home, a security guard for the community told me. Nearly 40 years ago, a coastal engineer had sized up this exact lot and written that the Pacific Ocean posed no threat of washing away the building or its septic system. Over the next week, the chasm beneath the street stretched below at least four waterfront houses and impeded emergency access to the area, forcing the city of Malibu to red-tag some 30 homes as uninhabitable. Cage did not respond to a request for comment. As an actor, he has infiltrated Alcatraz, navigated underground tunnels, and been pinned under rubble. During this real-life disaster, he was away. Not all of the homeowners in this gated community—a former mayor; the proprietor of a local Ford dealership; the president of the Miami Heat, Pat Riley—live there year-round. The security guard, Cesar Quintanilla, said that among the houses deemed unsafe, only four have full-time residents. When the Red Cross opened an emergency shelter at a nearby high school, nobody showed up. California’s shoreline faced considerable risk even before this year’s El Niño intensified, when a mass of abnormally warm water in the Pacific Ocean began moving east along the equator. When it hit South America, it cleaved in two, heading south and north. This pulse of warmer water, known as a Kelvin wave, at times this past summer added nearly a foot to tides in Southern California, Jonathan Warrick, a coastal scientist at the U.S. Geological Survey, told me. These conditions also tend to drum up storm activity in the Pacific, and earlier this month, three hurricanes were spinning simultaneously in the ocean. The one closest to California, Hurricane Marie, pushed the swell that hammered the coast over Labor Day weekend. Sea-level rise from global warming, too, is slowly adding inches of water that are raising the whole system, Warrick said. Malibu’s coastal-vulnerability report, published earlier this year, estimated that 1,410 of the city’s residential buildings—20 percent—plus more than half of the city’s commercial buildings could be affected this century by flooding, seawater intrusion, erosion, or other manifestations of rising seas. Malibu Mayor Bruce Silverstein expects that almost all waterfront structures will be in danger in the decades to come. “Nobody should be buying a home like that unless they can afford to lose it,” he told me. The victims in this situation don’t always get much sympathy, partly because many people assume that they can afford to swallow the costs. South of Los Angeles, in the city of Dana Point, nearly 20 waterfront homes got damaged or destroyed by high seas, and “we’re getting a lot of hate,” Natalie Driessen, a plastic surgeon whose home in a gated community along Beach Road has been damaged by the waves, told me. “A lot of people are saying, ‘Oh, let the rich homes fall in.’” Buying a home here costs $5 million or much more, but many people live in these houses year-round. Driessen, the daughter of a mechanic and a stay-at-home mom, said that she’d gotten to this neighborhood only after putting herself through medical school and working more than 100 hours a week while she had young kids at home. She said that dismissing the community’s plight is unfair. Even more galling to her and other homeowners is the feeling that authorities have abandoned them to the onrushing waves. When I visited Driessen’s home earlier this month, several neighbors and their contractors huddled among sandbags on what remained of her mangled patio. Every so often, a wave would thunder against a newly built pile of boulders in front of her house, dousing the group with mist and spray. For years, residents in this community of more than 180 homes on Beach Road have sought permission, in and out of court, from the California Coastal Commission to erect such defenses; many have built barriers without permits. The commission, a powerful state agency, rarely approves such projects: Seawalls can accelerate erosion and prevent the “natural inland migration of the beach,” the agency wrote in a letter to residents two years ago. It warned of potential fines, up to $11,250 a day, for unpermitted barriers. When the waves began ripping into homes in earnest earlier this month, the commission approved some emergency permits for 18-foot-high seawalls. The permits themselves cost $1,600 each, and homeowners rushed to pay the fee, then scrambled to find anyone who could throw down beach boulders in the narrow window between tides. The coastal commission has warned residents for years about the extreme risk they face living in a FEMA flood zone, one where the beach is eroding by about five feet a year. It “provided immediate and ongoing assistance” to homeowners, including issuing 24 emergency permits for barriers, an agency spokesperson, Joshua Smith, told me in a statement. “While seawalls can provide temporary relief for homes, they can also increase erosion and destroy the public beaches that help protect those same structures,” he noted. In front of Driessen’s home, contractors had started some of that work before nailing down the price, which, they told the group, could amount to more than $100,000 a home. Driessen didn’t see any alternative. “Just build the wall,” she told the contractors. “Build the wall.” In the longer term, Driessen and her neighbors want regular injections of fresh sand and a revetment—a sturdier, continuous barrier down the coast—but they have little guarantee that anything will change. In fact, the commission told homeowners that they’d have to remove within 120 days the boulders they’d already put down—again at their own expense—if the commission did not approve permits for a more permanent solution. The deck, kitchen, living room, and game room of Chris Rogers’s beachfront home got consumed by the waves before the contractors he’d hired could pour out concrete to defend the house. To save the rest of it, he told me, “we need immediate help.” Among the last homes to fall into the sea earlier this month, he said, was one whose owners had been in years-long talks with the coastal commission for protection. The most intense months are likely still to come. El Nino’s supercharged storms could soak parts of the state with heavy rains. Los Angeles is clearing storm drains and mountain reservoirs to try to prevent flooding. Up and down the coast, bulldozers and heavy machinery are moving rocks and building berms. In areas burned by wildfires, heavy rains can trigger landslides. The extreme weather is already clearing away the coastline. Driving down the Pacific Coast Highway in Malibu, I passed mile after mile of empty lots and the ruins of waterfront properties that burned in last year’s Palisades Fire. Of the roughly 300 homes along the beach that burned, none has been rebuilt. (The mayor told me that only 31 of them were owned by people who used them as their primary residence.) The people with multimillion-dollar homes on the beach may be making the most obvious sacrifices to El Niño, but all Californians are paying for damages. The residents on El Niño’s front lines have been peppering their elected officials with pleas for help; a bipartisan group of state legislators wrote to Governor Gavin Newsom asking him to declare a state emergency, which he did last week. Disaster in even the wealthiest enclaves can demand government resources. Taxpayers bear the brunt of repairs to infrastructure and public roads. Although many people want regular infusions of new sand and barriers, such solutions can overwhelm city and county budgets and cause unintended consequences elsewhere. Yet if the coast erodes away, everyone loses. Sandy beaches are an economic engine for Southern California, and denuding them drives away visitors. Few Californians want to face the prospect that beachfront homes may simply no longer be viable along stretches of the coast. Of the more than 180 homes on Beach Road in Dana Point, “I wouldn’t say all of them are vulnerable, but most of them would be,” John Gabbard, the city’s mayor, told me. “There’s going to be a very difficult long-term discussion about how do we protect—if we protect at all—homes that are built on the beach.” On two occasions in recent years, State Senator Ben Allen, a Democrat who represents Los Angeles County, has put forth legislation to create a loan program for local governments that want to buy beachfront homes and then rent them out to cover the cost of the program until the time comes to demolish them. Newsom vetoed it both times. “We have these beautiful coastal homes that are a part of California life. And we’ve all gotten used to this idea that people can live right up against the water and have these spectacular sunsets and have dinner with your toes in the sand,” Allen told me. But to him, how much society should pay to battle the sea is an open question. At some point, surely the price of building doomed houses is too high. For the moment, the reality of California’s coasts is that Francois Navarre, in one of the most desirable seaside enclaves in the world, is schlepping five-gallon jugs of water under the Malibu sun; he has no running water amid ongoing sinkhole repairs. He and his neighbors cannot rest easy. Another Kelvin wave, the largest and warmest one of the year, is making its way up the coast of Mexico and is expected to hit Los Angeles early next month. The king tides, the highest of the year, are landing around Thanksgiving and Christmas, and they happen to be the highest in an 18-year cycle. If more El Niño–juiced winter storms arrive, the ocean will almost certainly claim more homes. “They say that this is barely starting,” Quintanilla, the security guard, said. His job is to protect Sea Level Drive, but he cannot protect it from everything.

items.title: The Babies Left Behind in America
items.description: Photographs by Meridith Kohut Estela Garcia and 2-year-old Eber repeat their routine every morning: Around 8 a.m., he rustles her awake in the bed they share. She picks him up, changes his diaper, and pulls out a fresh set of tiny clothes. While Estela dresses him, Eber coos, “Mama, mama.” She smiles and strokes his cheeks, trying to hide her sadness at his confusion. Estela is 50 and has three sons, but Eber is not one of them. She’s been caring for him because ICE deported his parents to Venezuela, despite his mother’s pleas to be reunited first. Estela and her husband, Miguel, moved to Mobile, Alabama, 20 years ago to raise their own boys in a place that felt safe and had a slower rhythm than Las Vegas, where they’d met. Miguel works as a remodeling contractor. He spent years developing their four-acre property, building a wood shop, a chicken coop, and houses for two of their children (the third lives 15 minutes down the road). They bought peacocks as pets and planted bright perennial gardens, adorning them with stone fountains. By the driveway, they fly an American flag from an antique tractor. Over the years, their home evolved into a kind of retirement sanctuary—until this past winter, when it started to look like a day care. A police officer pulled over Eber’s mother, Marlyn, last November and, without accusing her of an infraction, turned her over to ICE, despite her work permit and pending asylum application. Eber, who had just finished breastfeeding, and his 7-year-old brother, Isaac, had nowhere to go. Marlyn’s 23-year-old cousin took the boys briefly. Then two of Marlyn’s friends—both undocumented—agreed to take one child each. Eber was moved into a rusty trailer with no heat; the woman watching him put socks on his hands to keep him warm. He was sick, but she was too scared of ICE to take him to a doctor. Isaac’s caregiver worked nights. Sometimes he made it to school; sometimes he didn’t. The boys needed a better home. Frantic phone calls among Marlyn’s friends and co-workers eventually led to Estela. They had all worked together at a plant nursery, and Estela was the only American citizen they knew. She agreed to take the boys and then return them to Marlyn, not knowing that doing the right thing would go so wrong: that county officials would end up investigating her for trafficking; that her bank account would dwindle to almost nothing; that Eber would still be in her home, unable to remember his own mother, nearly a year after she was picked up. “I’ve lost a lot of weight because it’s so stressful,” Estela told me, sitting in her living room. Eber was clinging to her, his face buried in her chest. “My family is like, ‘What have you done?’ ” President Trump’s rush to deport as many immigrants as possible is creating a new family-separation crisis. Whereas his first administration took children from their parents at the border to deter illegal crossings, the second is separating families living in the United States as part of a purge. Like last time, Trump officials claim that this is untrue. But stories like Eber’s are not hard to find, as I learned this year while reporting on immigration enforcement in Alabama, California, Illinois, Missouri, and Texas. [ From the September 2022 issue: Caitlin Dickerson on the secret history of family separation ] As of April, the Brookings Institution put the total number of affected children at about 205,000—71 percent of whom are U.S. citizens. Most of those cases involve the loss of one parent, a devastating blow to families. But the Brookings researchers believe that more than 35,000 of the cases are like Eber’s, in which a child has been left with no parent at all. Since the analysis was published, the pace of ICE arrests has increased. In July, the agency arrested a record 49,000 people, a majority of whom have no criminal record, according to a New York Times review of data obtained by the Deportation Data Project. Many of the people ICE is targeting entered the United States legally, through parole programs or by requesting asylum, and were in the process of working toward permanent legal immigration status. (A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson told me the Deportation Data Project’s numbers are “inaccurate” but did not correct them, adding that a pending application for legal status does not shield immigrants from arrest.) In recent years, ICE policy required officers to either reunite detained parents with their children before deportation or confirm that the children had an official caregiver in their parents’ absence. But in July 2025, DHS revised the policy, sprinkling it with caveats, such as “when operationally feasible,” that appear to allow officers to prioritize the speed and volume of deportations over everything else—including the children whom deportees leave behind. Meridith Kohut for The Atlantic Estela talks with Eber’s mother, Marlyn, who was deported to Venezuela in February, and the social worker Shaina Simenas on a video call. The result is tens of thousands of children being shuffled among the houses of anxious temporary caregivers. It can take months to procure the passports, visas, and other permissions necessary to transport children to their parents, many of whom have been deported to countries whose governments can’t help, or won’t. This past spring, the United Nations’ International Organization for Migration reunified 12 children with their deported families using funding from the U.S. State Department, according to a UN official, who added that the organization has received requests to help other children, but they lack the proper paperwork. Some children end up with foster families after caregivers burn out, and some have landed in the homes of abusive relatives or acquaintances. In January, 2-year-old Orlin Hernandez Reyes was left with his aunt’s ex-partner, who was known to be dangerous, when ICE detained his mother. She begged deportation officers to reunite her with Orlin before she was deported to Honduras, but that didn’t happen. Soon after, Orlin’s body was found with broken bones and signs of sexual abuse, and his caregiver was charged with murder. (He has pleaded not guilty.) Then–ICE Director Todd Lyons blamed his mother , saying that she “chose to leave her son here with a violent murderer who took his life.” Even children like Eber, who land in a safe place, are likely to experience long-term psychological harm from separation. “To have such a huge number of children forced into a traumatic situation because of some policy—it’s really kind of unimaginable,” Wendy Smith, a retired associate dean at the University of Southern California’s school of social work and a co-founder of the nonprofit National Foster Youth Institute, told me. We are “creating a whole class of children who are going to grow up with all sorts of problems.” (The DHS spokesperson said that the agency “does not separate families or deport U.S. citizens” and that, absent indications of abuse or neglect, parents “can choose to take their children with them.”) There are key differences between the family separations happening now and those of the first Trump administration. In 2017 and 2018, career bureaucrats worked from within the government to try to prevent separations, alert the press when they happened, and reunite families under court orders that high-level DHS officials were trying to defy. But many civil servants deemed insufficiently loyal to Trump were fired en masse during the early months of his second term. Since then, the White House has sent a clear message that pushing back on mass deportation will cost you your job. Also different: The separations of the first Trump administration were the result of a distinct policy (“Zero Tolerance”) that, once brought to light, could be challenged in federal court. Today, family separations appear to be incidental—the consequence of a ruthless effort to hit a quota, no matter the cost. And this time, people with firsthand knowledge of separations are keeping quiet. Many temporary caregivers are undocumented themselves or have relatives who are; they worry that drawing attention would put their own families at risk. Government and nonprofit workers are also scared to speak up. The White House has attacked organizations that oppose its goals by cutting funding, launching dubious criminal investigations, and issuing retaliatory executive orders. “In a lot of jurisdictions, people don’t want to write anything down,” Maria Cancian, a Georgetown University economist who co-authored the Brookings study, told me. She and her colleagues spoke with caseworkers in more than half a dozen states who had assisted separated families; they agreed to communicate only because she did not plan to disclose their identities or locations in her report. “Why would you volunteer any information that makes you more of a target?” said Cancian, a former Obama appointee in the Department of Health and Human Services who helped oversee children in immigration custody. Alabama, where Estela lives, has an estimated 70,000 undocumented immigrants. Many are concentrated near Mobile, where they work at plant nurseries, shipyards, construction sites, and fish-packing plants. On a visit there over the summer, I was barraged with stories of parents swept up in ICE raids, leaving children marooned with relatives or neighbors who were unprepared to care for them. These arrests were a constant topic of discussion in churches, at dinner tables, during school drop-offs. Everywhere I went, cellphones buzzed with information about immigration checkpoints and intersections where local police seemed to be pulling over anyone who was visibly Latino. Meridith Kohut for The Atlantic Estela’s husband, Miguel, plays with Eber outside their home in Mobile, Alabama. A woman named Josefa told me that she and her relatives were taking turns caring for their nieces and nephews—ages 9, 7, and 1—because they could afford only a few days of diapers and extra food at a time. A 15-year-old girl was living alone in a squalid trailer because her father had been detained, and his last paycheck was running out. When Miguel, Estela’s husband, got home from work one evening, I asked if he would call around to co-workers and friends to see if they knew of any other displaced children. “Oh yeah,” the first man he called said. “My wife and I also have two little girls.” The police officer did not tell Marlyn why he’d pulled her over on a grocery run outside Mobile—but he asked if she was in the United States illegally. She pulled out her phone to show him that she’d attended all her ICE check-ins, and that her asylum case was scheduled to be heard in June. “The immigration judge wants to talk to you,” the officer said, as Marlyn recalled when I first spoke with her, earlier this summer. “I don’t understand,” she replied. “I haven’t done anything wrong.” “Don’t worry, they’re not going to deport you,” the officer said. Of course they are , she thought. Marlyn says she asked the officer if they could pick up her children because they were at home with a roommate who wasn’t prepared to care for them indefinitely. He refused. She spent about an hour in the Mobile County Metro Jail, followed by 10 days in an ICE detention center in Mississippi. Then she was transferred to the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center, a 1,000-bed facility 90 miles west of Baton Rouge. Marlyn’s family had arrived at the southern border in May 2023, as Venezuela devolved into chaos under Nicolás Maduro’s regime. A friend had told them that there was work for new immigrants in Mobile. They rented a house and found jobs—Marlyn at the nursery and her husband, Jesus, at Walmart. In April 2024, Jesus got into an altercation with a co-worker, was charged with a misdemeanor for reckless endangerment, and was deported to Venezuela. With two young children to support, Marlyn leaned on other immigrant families for help. She felt adrift but was getting by, until five months later, when she was pulled over on the grocery run. At the facility in Louisiana, she spoke with an immigration lawyer who told her that she had virtually no chance of getting out on bail under the Trump administration’s policies. The lawyer said she could spend up to two years detained while she waited for a decision in her case, which she was likely to lose anyway. Marlyn had heard that people who agreed to be deported could request to be reunited with their children beforehand, so she decided to give up her asylum case. She started sending ICE officials three messages a day—the maximum allowed—asking to be deported with Eber and Isaac. “I told them, ‘I have my two children. One is a little baby who was born here. I have no one to take care of them. They’re going to be left alone,’ ” she recalled, adding: “They just kept giving the same response—that they were going to work on it. But they never did anything.” (DHS did not comment on individual cases in this story.) In detention, Marlyn worried about Isaac and Eber constantly. Eber was weak and small for his age; he’d been born with a cyst in his lung that still needed to be surgically removed. She would fear the worst anytime Estela didn’t answer the phone. “It’s agonizing not knowing about your children,” Marlyn said. She befriended other mothers in detention. Some had been there for many months. She saw them faint and have panic attacks. One told Marlyn she had been arrested while taking her 10-day-old baby to the doctor. Early one morning in February, three months into her detention, a staff member woke Marlyn and said she was being deported. Her time had run out. She had to board a plane back to Venezuela, and leave her kids behind. Trump’s immigration crackdown has sent countless families into crisis. Sharon Balmer Cartagena, a family lawyer in Los Angeles, has had to deliver bad news to parents over and over, with the help of her colleagues at Public Counsel, the largest pro bono law firm in the country. They told one mother, who’d tried to create an emergency plan in case she was detained, that she’d filed the wrong paperwork in court and accidentally given up her parental rights. They told another mother from Mexico, whose ex-wife had cut off contact as soon as she was deported, that the best she could hope for was one or two weeks of court-ordered visitations a year. And they told a mother from Haiti—who was so scared of being deported that she preemptively moved to Mexico—that she may never see her child again; the estranged father had agreed to care for their 3-year-old temporarily, but then blocked the mother’s phone number as soon as she arrived in Mexico. “We had to explain to her, ‘There’s nothing we can do. You have no viable pathway to regain any kind of contact with your child,’ ” Cartagena told me. “It was horrific.” [ From the April 2026 issue: Caitlin Dickerson on how the Cruz family decided to self-deport ] These cases fall into a gray area between immigration law and family law. This means that many of the families ICE is separating will need not one but two lawyers to try to get their children back—and there isn’t enough legal help to go around. Cartagena has tried to recruit more family lawyers to help with immigration cases, without much success. “I’m trying to be like, ‘Everybody, there’s a family-law emergency here!’ ” she said. “Everyone’s busy.” Meridith Kohut for The Atlantic Attorney Sharon Balmer Cartagena in her home office in L.A. Cartagena grew up in Reading, Pennsylvania, one of the poorest cities in America, and saw how much her classmates were traumatized when child-welfare agencies broke up their families—often because the adults were too poor to provide for their children, not because they were unfit parents. She went to law school hoping to help children in foster care. Her career has tracked a period of growing consensus that this kind of family separation often does more harm than good; foster-care systems around the country have been shrinking and state agencies have been directed to keep children in their home whenever possible. But under the first and second Trump administrations, separations have become more common for parents who are detained by immigration authorities. Cartagena first discovered how complicated these separations were in 2018, when she became a directing attorney at Public Counsel. Immigration lawyers started contacting her, asking for help with clients who had been separated from their children under the Zero Tolerance policy. The parents had been allowed to return to the United States under a federal-court settlement, but enough time had passed that some children had been deemed wards of the state, while others had new legal guardians. Family-court judges were blocking their reunifications. Cartagena explained that family courts exist to protect children whose parents have been accused of abuse or neglect; the system is not set up to deal with parents who face none of these allegations but lose custody because they have been deported. She helped one mother regain custody of her teenage daughter, but the process took more than a year. Others never had their parental rights restored. When I first spoke with Cartagena this year, she was working with a mother named Magdalena Callejas, who had full custody of her 4- and 6-year-old children in March 2024, when she was arrested at a Border Patrol checkpoint in Texas. Magdalena had a pending visa application. Her ex-partner was undocumented, with multiple DUIs; Magdalena had a restraining order against him for abusing her and her son from a previous relationship. But after ICE detained her, he took the 4- and 6-year-old back. She was powerless to stop it. Magdalena says she asked ICE officials to reunite her with her children but was told the agency “did not do that.” She agreed to leave the country voluntarily, hoping to get her children back as soon as she arrived in El Salvador. In the meantime, her ex filed for custody. An immigration lawyer who met Magdalena in detention contacted Cartagena, who explained that because Magdalena was unavailable to care for the children, the father was within his rights. In court, Magdalena’s ex argued that he was a changed man, and that unsafe conditions in El Salvador outweighed his criminal past. The trial dragged on for months. The judge ordered the children into the custody of a neutral caregiver; when she was no longer willing to help, the judge sent the children to another home. On video calls during the father’s court-ordered visits, Magdalena’s children used a shorthand to tell her that he was still drinking: “Dad went to get some juice.” Cartagena shared all of this with the court but still didn’t know how the judge was going to rule. Most family-court judges aren’t familiar with immigration law, or accustomed to granting custody to a parent in another country. The longer a separation lasts, the harder it is to reverse; Cartagena said that family-court judges often defer to the status quo rather than disrupt a child’s living arrangements a second time—even if it means keeping them from their biological parent, or a parent who is more fit to care for them. Despite Magdalena’s ex’s history of abuse, Cartagena worried that she could still end up permanently separated from her children. “If she doesn’t win,” Cartagena said, “what do I tell everyone else?” A judge eventually ordered that Magdalena’s children be returned to her in El Salvador after a 30-day legal stay to allow her ex-husband to appeal. He had stopped submitting weekly alcohol tests, which Cartagena believes may have swayed the judge. But that same day, the children’s caregiver said she was fed up. She was going to drop them off at a police station if no one retrieved them. So even though the judge renewed Magdalena’s five-year restraining order against her ex, he also ordered the father to pick up and care for the children until Cartagena could raise money and find a volunteer to transport them to El Salvador. There was nowhere else for the children to go but back to their father. Cartagena has a tattoo on her wrist of a mama bear and two cubs—one for each of her children, who are 11 and 14. “I couldn’t imagine if I couldn’t see my kids or I didn’t know where they were,” she said. Sometimes the best advice she can offer detained parents is to get their children out of the United States as quickly as possible, before anyone can intervene. She’s helped procure travel documents and recruit volunteers to shuttle children across borders to their deported parents, including an 18-month-old and a 3-year-old who were sent to Peru in May. She also ghostwrites emails to ICE on behalf of immigration lawyers who want to pressure the agency to reunify families before a parent is deported. Since Trump took office a second time, she has started waking up to answer emails at 5 a.m. instead of 6. She works every weekend. And she began raising money so that Public Counsel can start a five-person division focused on immigrant-family separations. “We’re all doing this on top of our regular work,” Cartagena said. (She recently became the executive director of LevittQuinn, another family-law legal-aid organization in L.A., but will continue partnering with Public Counsel in her work on immigrant-family separations.) She and her colleagues have held dozens of trainings across Los Angeles for immigrant parents. I attended one at an elementary school in Boyle Heights, an immigrant enclave and a hot spot for ICE raids. A dozen people sat in plastic chairs, their eyes darting to the door each time someone entered. One of Cartagena’s colleagues told the group to be careful about paperwork; well-meaning immigration lawyers had been giving clients a “temporary guardianship” form, which isn’t valid in some states. She urged the parents to arrange a caregiver, a backup caregiver, and a backup for the backup. People burn out or give up, and if there is no plan, the children are left in limbo. A mother raised her hand. “The only people I know are like me,” she said. “They’re also undocumented.” Another said: “I don’t have anyone. What do I do?” I found a family with no backup plan in the spring, when I went to Honduras to interview deportees as they arrived by the planeful from ICE detention centers. A father named Edwin said that after three years of meticulously following the government’s requests to further his family’s asylum case, his wife, Sarah, was thinking about going into hiding; she didn’t want to be picked up by ICE and have to leave her children alone. [ Read: A new kind of family-separation crisis ] When I went to visit Sarah in May, in a Dallas suburb, her 4-year-old son, Johnny, answered the door and asked me: “Do you know when my dad is coming home?” Before I could answer, Johnny continued: “Do you know what happened to him?” He repeated versions of these questions over the two days of my visit. “Do you know where my dad is? Do you know if he’s okay?” When the questions would start, Johnny’s 12-year-old sister, Katie, tried to distract him with coloring books and screens. Recently, he’d had an hours-long meltdown when Sarah tried to donate some of Edwin’s work clothes that were crowding the closet. Every afternoon he sits at the front window waiting for his dad’s truck to pull up outside. While reporting this story, I talked with other families with credible asylum cases who were considering going underground to avoid being separated from their children, knowing that it would likely sabotage their chances of ever gaining legal status. This is the bracing irony of Trump’s deportation campaign: Its goal is to crack down on lawbreaking, but its implementation is encouraging it. Immigrants who have complied with the law are being targeted, and they are choosing to hide, despite the fear and stress, because the alternatives are worse: abandoning their children, or being deported with them to dangerous places. Sarah and Edwin have been running from MS‑13 since 2013, when Sarah witnessed a murder in Honduras. Gang members wrongly assumed that she had testified against the killer and started threatening her. In 2022, they showed up at a relative’s house and killed a young woman, likely mistaking her for Sarah. She and Edwin decided it was time to go. They requested asylum and were admitted across the border during the Biden administration and moved to the Dallas suburbs. Edwin started working in construction and Sarah worked nights as a janitor. They rarely saw each other, but their schedules ensured that one of them was always home with the kids. (I’m using pseudonyms for this family because of ongoing threats.) In January, the four of them went to an ICE office for a routine check-in. Edwin was detained without explanation. Sarah and the kids were distraught, and hoped it was a mistake. She planned to sell their cars to cover the cost of Edwin’s bond, but then he was transferred from a detention center in Texas to one in Mississippi. There, he checked the agency’s online portal for detainees and saw that he was being deported for allegedly skipping a court appointment that he had not been given the chance to attend. (The DHS spokesperson said the agency affords immigrants due process.) “If we hadn’t gone to the check-in, my husband would be here,” Sarah told me. “It would have been better if we did things the wrong way.” Without Edwin, Sarah felt forced to take a series of risks. She didn’t have a license but started driving herself to work, because she was now solely responsible for paying the bills. She skipped her next check-in with ICE and, knowing that officers might come looking for her, moved apartments without telling the government. She started leaving Katie in charge of her younger brother while she was at work. “My daughter’s teacher said I shouldn’t tell anyone, because they could be taken away from me,” Sarah said. Without child care, Sarah installed cameras in the apartment and watched the kids on her phone, in between cleaning toilets and vacuuming. Katie would fall asleep as soon as she left for work. Johnny, who was used to sleeping in his father’s arms, would pace the house every night. One time, Sarah saw him jamming an air freshener into an electrical outlet, which started to spark and smoke. Katie slept through the sound of her mother’s phone calls. Meridith Kohut for The Atlantic Johnny and Katie settle down for the night as their father, whose face has been blurred to protect his identity, watches via video call from Honduras. Sarah changed her schedule to work one overnight shift during the week and double shifts on Saturdays and Sundays. Edwin started watching the children on video calls from Honduras while she was gone. On the first evening that I visited, he called while she was making dinner. “Have you eaten, my love?” she asked him. “Not yet. I’m still working,” he said. Then he pointed the phone at a young man crouched on a hillside just outside the house, looking over the village below. “They’re here watching.” “Put it down! Put it down!” Sarah told him. “Don’t let him see you.” MS‑13 patrols their community, setting curfews and extorting people. Sarah and Edwin weren’t sure if the gang had realized that he was back. They were looking for a place to hide if Sarah ends up being deported, but nowhere in Central America seemed safe. Sarah scarfed down some shrimp pasta. Katie cut Johnny’s food and tried to keep him in his chair. “She’s become my right hand,” Sarah told me of her 12-year-old. She looked at the clock and determined that she had time for a quick nap. She went into the bedroom and set a timer on her phone for 27 minutes. Katie started doing the dishes. She packed some leftover pasta into a Tupperware container for her mom and placed it in Sarah’s backpack with two bottles of water and a ziplock bag of cookies. Sarah sprang up when her alarm went off. Her eyes were red and wet. She threw on her uniform—khakis and a polo shirt—and brushed her hair back into a ponytail. She called the kids into the bedroom and told them to put their pajamas on while she did her makeup. They climbed into bed and Katie dialed Edwin, then propped her phone up against a lamp so that he could watch them after they fell asleep. A minute later, Johnny was out of bed, pacing. When Sarah finished getting ready, she gathered him in her arms and placed him next to his sister. She looked into the camera at Edwin and said, “Okay, you’re in charge now.” Marlyn has been living a version of Sarah’s nightmare since she arrived back in Venezuela in February, with video calls as the only portal to her children. She and Jesus moved back into their family home in Guanare, a small city about six hours by car from Caracas. Jesus struggled to find work and Marlyn spent most of her days trying to figure out how to reunite with her sons. Back in Mobile, Eber demanded to be held constantly, screaming every time Estela put him down. Isaac would hyperventilate and hide anytime someone mentioned ICE. He started acting out in school. Estela was called in for a meeting with his teachers, during which she explained that she was trying to figure out how to get the boys back to Marlyn. This only seemed to make things worse. A county social worker showed up at her house unannounced, asking questions: Where were the boys sleeping? What did they eat? Did they have clean clothes? A few days later, the social worker called and threatened to take the boys from her. “You don’t know what you’re getting yourself into,” the social worker said, according to Estela. “If you don’t have custody and their parents aren’t here, the state has the right to take them.” “I just wanted to do something good,” Estela told her, “and everyone is making it seem like I’m doing something wrong.” She called Marlyn in a panic. After her own experience in detention, Marlyn was terrified of her children ending up in government custody. Estela tried to reassure Marlyn that she wouldn’t let anyone take the boys. But she was also scared that she might not be able to stop it from happening. Tension was building between the two women. Estela despaired about giving up her life to take care of Eber and Isaac. All of her time, and a lot of her money, was going toward the boys’ needs: clothes, school supplies, food, medication. Marlyn, who had no way to repay her, was grateful for the help and embarrassed by how much she needed it. She also worried that her children were becoming too attached to Estela. “She was scared I would keep her kids,” Estela told me. “I said, ‘No, I would never do that, because I’m also a mom.’ ” But she knew that sending the boys to Venezuela could traumatize them all over again. She put Eber in day care so they wouldn’t grow too close. Eber couldn’t travel until he’d had lung surgery; his doctors said the cyst would become cancerous if it wasn’t removed, and getting the procedure in Venezuela would be nearly impossible. And no airline would be willing to fly Isaac out of the country without a legal guardian or passport. Estela made dozens of calls to lawyers and nonprofit groups. She contacted ICE offices in Georgia and Alabama but received no response. Finally she reached an official in Chicago who said that if she turned Isaac over to the government, he could be deported back to Venezuela within a few weeks. It seemed like the only option. Estela asked Isaac’s father to explain the plan to his son over a video call. Jesus told Isaac that he was going to a shelter with other children who were waiting to be returned to their parents. “You are going to be okay,” he said. “Nothing bad is going to happen to you.” Marlyn and Estela repeated the reassurances until Isaac was willing to go. In late April, Estela loaded a backpack with clothes and snacks. The next morning, she put a piece of paper with phone numbers into Isaac’s shirt pocket and told him not to lose it. She drove him two and a half hours to the closest ICE field office, in southern Louisiana. They said they loved each other. A couple of hours later, she got a text from ICE saying that Isaac was on a plane to a foster home in Texas, where the 7-year-old would wait until he could go before an immigration judge and formally request “voluntary departure” to Venezuela. Meridith Kohut for The Atlantic Estela greets Miguel as he arrives home from work. Caring for Eber has drained their bank account. Estela returned to Mobile, and to Eber’s more complicated situation. He needed surgery, and his travel would be harder to arrange than Isaac’s. He was a U.S. citizen, so he couldn’t enter Venezuela without a visa—which requires a parent’s permission and usually their presence. Meanwhile, most construction work around Mobile was on hold because workers were too scared to leave their houses. Miguel’s business was suffering, but Estela couldn’t help, because she had no time to work. And soon after she began to look into travel documents for Eber, the police started showing up at her house. The sheriff’s deputy at the door said he was looking for Isaac. Estela started to explain the situation all over again, but her heart was racing. She worried that the officer didn’t understand or believe her, so she called Shaina Simenas, a social worker at the Young Center for Immigrant Children’s Rights. “Okay, put him on the phone,” Simenas said. She told the officer that Isaac was in federal custody and that ICE had deported both of his parents. He seemed satisfied, but officers returned to Estela’s house twice, until finally Simenas persuaded the department to close its investigation. The Young Center normally advocates for unaccompanied children in their immigration proceedings, but when family separations began to accelerate after Trump took office for the second time, it assigned a team of six to focus on them. Since then, they’ve worked on more than 150 cases and have a growing waitlist. “It’s a drop in the bucket compared to the need,” Kelly Kribs, one of the team’s co-directors, told me. Even without advertising this work, the Young Center has been overwhelmed. Some children and detained parents have found them by word of mouth. “We got a call from a 17-year-old boy a few weeks ago who was looking for help because his mom was his only caregiver, and he’s couch surfing in upstate New York,” Kribs said. “I think he Googled us.” Kribs and her colleagues have tried to advocate for a number of women who were still breastfeeding when they were detained, despite an ICE policy against such detainments outside “exceptional circumstances.” One mother from St. Louis who had no criminal history was detained at three months postpartum. ICE ignored the Young Center’s request to release her under the policy. It took days for Simenas and a colleague to set up an account on the detainee tablet system, so she could message her family. “She went weeks without even seeing her infant because of how nonfunctional the system is for these families,” Simenas told me. The Young Center has also tried to support temporary caregivers who are so overwhelmed that the children are unsafe. Kribs told me about a man in Florida who’d had to quit his job to care for five children, including a six-month-old, after their mothers—the man’s girlfriend and her sister—were detained. He had no income to pay for food and diapers. “He was father to none of these children,” Kribs said. One Illinois woman taking care of a 5-year-old boy whose father had been deported to Mexico was so financially strapped that she became homeless; she sent the child to sleep at a friend’s apartment while she lived in her car. Kribs eventually persuaded ICE to transport the boy back to his father. But first she had to send the caregiver $20 in gas money so the boy could be handed off. On rare occasions, Kribs and her colleagues have transported children themselves, as in the case of a 13-month-old girl they ferried back to Mexico last year. Kribs said the reunion was bittersweet: The baby’s mother was waiting at the airport with balloons and a giant stuffed animal. But the little girl, who had spent more than half her life separated from her mother, didn’t seem to recognize her. Now that ICE is almost solely dedicated to maximizing deportations, Kribs said, few people are left at the agency who will listen to their concerns. When possible, the Young Center tries to work with contractors to encourage ICE to comply with the policy on reunifying parents and children, or sorting out custody before deporting them. But not every detention center has enough staff to handle those requests, and some are busier than others. Kribs said that trying to appeal to deportation officers, who are under the most pressure to hit the president’s numerical goals, is especially challenging. One officer admitted to her that he thought it was “just so much easier when they leave their kids here,” she recalled. “Like it’s a logistical headache for them to try not to separate families.” (DHS did not comment on this claim.) Separated parents have told me their pain is all-consuming. Before she was deported, a mother named Lucía called me from the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center, crying about not having seen her 14-month-old and 3-year-old in three months. She said it was excruciating not being able to explain to them why she was gone. “They’re babies,” she said. “They don’t understand.” Lucía said that most of the women around her were in similar situations. Some had a spouse who was with their children, but other kids were staying with extended relatives or acquaintances. “In this room where I am,” she said, “there are 56 of us, and the majority are moms.” After just over a month in federal custody in Texas, Isaac landed at the airport in La Guaira, Venezuela , in May. When Eber had his surgery, also in the spring, Estela spent three days and nights in a chair next to his hospital bed. She sent pictures to Marlyn and Jesus to keep them updated. Marlyn said very little in response. Not being able to be with Eber had left her speechless. “Thank you, Estela,” Jesus replied in one message. “I don’t know how, but one day I’m going to repay you for everything you’ve done for my son.” Estela promised Marlyn that she wouldn’t hand off Eber to another caretaker, and that she’d get him back to Venezuela. But she’s exhausted. She feels like she’s neglecting her sons and her husband. Recently their bank account was down to $27. She used to go to church four times a week, but now manages just one. In the pews, she asks God to allow Eber to return to his family, and for the patience to keep caring for him in the meantime. “This baby needs to be with his mother,” she said. Meridith Kohut for The Atlantic After a year of separation, Eber seems to no longer remember Marlyn and calls ­Estela “Mama.” Estela has been trying to arrange Eber’s transfer to Venezuela all year. During a video call with Marlyn in August, he sat on a couch next to Estela, picking Lucky Charms out of a bowl. For 10 long minutes, Estela cajoled him to say hello or blow his mom a kiss. He only glanced at the camera, and didn’t seem to recognize Marlyn’s face or voice. When I speak with Marlyn by phone now, her speech is slow and soft, almost zombie-like. She says she can’t sleep. Venezuelan officials said that they would add her name to a list of parents who need their children back from the U.S., but they have not given her a timeline for Eber’s return. She calls them every day, but they tell her to keep waiting. She stays in touch with mothers she met in detention, and they update one another on trying to get their children back. So far, Isaac is the only success story among them. Meanwhile, Marlyn didn’t see Eber’s first steps or hear his first words. He was so fragile the last time they were together. Now he’s much bigger, with a mischievous smile that she’s never seen in person. He launches himself into bear hugs that she’s never felt. Even if he makes it to Venezuela, they’ll never regain the time they lost. “I’ve missed everything,” she said. This article appears in the November 2026 print edition with the headline “The Babies Left Behind in America.”

items.title: CEMAC : la COBAC et les banques planchent sur les risques ESG et l’intelligence artificielle à Malabo
items.description: © DR La 15e réunion annuelle de concertation entre le Président de la COBAC et la profession bancaire et financière de la CEMAC s'est tenue le 25 septembre 2026 à Malabo, sous la présidence de Yvon Sana Bangui, Gouverneur de la BEAC. Gouvernance, résilience financière et transformation numérique au menu. Le secteur bancaire régional face à ses mutations. La 15ème Réunion annuelle de concertation du Président de la COBAC avec la profession bancaire et financière de la CEMAC s'est tenue le 25 septembre 2026 à Malabo, en Guinée équatoriale, sous la présidence de M. Yvon SANA BANGUI, Gouverneur de la BEAC et Président de la COBAC. Les échanges ont porté sur les principaux enjeux auxquels fait face le secteur bancaire régional : gouvernance et risques ESG, stress tests et résilience financière, évolution des services de paiement et intelligence artificielle. Les participants ont notamment souligné la nécessité de renforcer les dispositifs de gestion des risques, d'accompagner la transformation numérique, de consolider la sécurité des paiements et de développer les compétences nécessaires à l'utilisation responsable des nouvelles technologies. À la clôture des travaux, l'accent a été mis sur le renforcement de la gouvernance, de la résilience et de la maîtrise des risques, afin d'accompagner les transformations du secteur tout en préservant la stabilité du système bancaire et financier régional, dans un contexte marqué par l'innovation et les exigences climatiques. items.title: Tunisie : le durcissement migratoire fait reculer les départs, mais pousse les réseaux de passeurs dans la clandestinité
items.description: La pression exercee par les autorites tunisiennes sur les migrants subsahariens et les reseaux de passeurs a profondement transforme les routes migratoires passant par la Tunisie. C'est l'un des principaux constats du rapport publie en septembre 2026 par la Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), consacre a l'evolution de l'ecosysteme du trafic de migrants en Tunisie entre janvier 2025 et juin 2026. Depuis le durcissement de la politique migratoire amorce en 2023, Tunis a multiplie les interceptions en mer, les operations de demantelement des campements informels, les controles a l'interieur du pays, les expulsions vers les frontieres algerienne et libyenne ainsi que les retours vers les pays d'origine. Cette strategie a effectivement reduit le nombre de migrants parvenant a rejoindre l'Europe depuis la Tunisie. Selon les donnees du Haut-Commissariat des Nations unies pour les refugies (HCR) citees par la GI-TOC, 4 861 personnes arrivees en Italie en 2025 etaient parties de Tunisie, contre 19 460 en 2024, soit une baisse de 75 %. Par rapport au pic de 2023, ou 97 667 arrivees depuis la Tunisie avaient ete enregistrees, le recul atteint environ 95 %. La tendance s'est poursuivie au premier semestre 2026, avec seulement 1 074 arrivees depuis la Tunisie, contre 1 966 durant la meme periode de 2025. Une baisse des arrivees qui masque une demande toujours presente Pour la GI-TOC, cette diminution ne signifie toutefois pas que la demande de passage a disparu. Le rapport estime entre 16 000 et 18 000 les tentatives de traversee en 2025, auxquelles s'ajoutent au moins 3 602 tentatives au cours des trois premiers mois de 2026. Les auteurs parlent ainsi d'une mobilite « reprimee » par les controles plutot que d'une disparition durable de la pression migratoire. Les controles ont reduit les possibilites de passage, mais les facteurs qui poussent les migrants a partir restent presents. La Tunisie demeure notamment moins coûteuse que la Libye pour rejoindre l'Europe. Le rapport estime le prix d'une traversee depuis la Tunisie entre 450 et 600 euros, contre au moins 1 000 euros depuis certaines zones de depart libyennes. Cette persistance de la demande a contraint les reseaux de passeurs a se reorganiser. Des reseaux plus petits et plus difficiles a detecter Selon le rapport, les structures relativement visibles et organisees qui operaient auparavant ont progressivement laisse place a des groupes plus petits et plus flexibles. Les recrutements et la coordination passent davantage par des plateformes de messagerie chiffree, tandis que des ressortissants subsahariens jouent desormais un role accru d'intermediaires au sein des communautes migrantes. La GI-TOC observe notamment une implication croissante de ressortissants guineens, ivoiriens, camerounais, senegalais et soudanais dans l'organisation des departs. Les organisateurs tunisiens conserveraient cependant une partie du controle logistique, tandis que les migrants et autres acteurs subsahariens occupent davantage les fonctions les plus exposees au risque d'arrestation. Cette evolution a aussi touche la fabrication des embarcations. Depuis les operations de repression engagees fin 2023, la construction des bateaux metalliques se serait deplacee des ateliers tunisiens vers les campements de migrants, notamment dans les oliveraies de la region de Sfax. Certains bateaux peuvent etre assembles en deux jours, selon le rapport. Ce recours accru a la clandestinite a un coût humain. La fragmentation des reseaux reduit la possibilite pour les migrants de verifier la fiabilite ou l'experience des passeurs et des capitaines. Le rapport fait etat de bateaux surcharges, moins bien equipes et de departs organises dans des conditions destinees a echapper aux controles, ce qui accroît le risque d'accidents et complique les operations de secours. Du controle des cotes au report des risques Le meme phenomene s'observe aux frontieres terrestres. Le modele du drop-and-walk , dans lequel les migrants sont deposes pres de la frontiere puis poursuivent a pied, reste utilise. La GI-TOC rapporte que le deplacement des points de depot vers des secteurs plus recules allonge les trajets et augmente les risques d'epuisement, de desorientation, d'agression et d'extorsion. Le rapport fait egalement etat de cas d'enlevements contre rancon dans l'ouest de la Tunisie, notamment dans les gouvernorats de Kasserine, du Kef et de Siliana. Le demantelement des campements de migrants a Sfax illustre cette dynamique. Les operations menees a partir de mars 2025 auraient deplace environ 7 000 personnes, principalement des migrants subsahariens. Selon la GI-TOC, ces operations ont surtout conduit a une dispersion des migrants vers de plus petites installations ou vers les zones urbaines, plutot qu'a une disparition de leur presence. Une politique efficace sur les chiffres, mais qui transforme le marche clandestin Le bilan dresse par la GI-TOC est donc contraste. Sur le plan quantitatif, le dispositif tunisien a considerablement reduit les departs reussis vers l'Italie et les entrees irregulieres sur le territoire. Mais cette contraction s'est accompagnee d'une transformation du marche du passage clandestin. Le rapport estime ainsi que la Tunisie est passee d'une importante zone de depart vers l'Europe a un corridor de transit a faible volume mais a haut risque. La baisse des arrivees en Italie constitue donc un indicateur reel du recul des passages, mais elle ne permet pas, a elle seule, de conclure a la disparition du phenomene de trafic de migrants.

items.title: Violences basées sur le genre : le PNUD et le VNU brisent le silence à Yaoundé
items.description: © DR Dans le cadre de la Semaine d'action pour les ODD, le PNUD et le Programme des Volontaires des Nations Unies au Cameroun ont organisé une mini-conférence à Playce Yaoundé dédiée à la lutte contre les violences basées sur le genre, réunissant MINPROFF, activistes et partenaires autour du dialogue et de l'action. Briser le silence, agir ensemble. Le PNUD et le Programme VNU Cameroun ont réuni des représentants du MINPROFF, des activistes et des partenaires pour une mini-conférence à Playce Yaoundé dans le cadre de la Semaine d'action pour les ODD, créant un espace de dialogue et d'action sur les violences basées sur le genre (VBG). La session a été animée par le Représentant Résident Adjoint du PNUD Martin Hart-Hansen, le Directeur Pays du Programme VNU Raoul Bersha et la Présidente de l'association Afiri Yvonne Balema, qui ont guidé les discussions sur la prévention, la sensibilisation et l'action collective. L'échange a été l'occasion de partager des expériences, de faire entendre les voix et de renforcer les partenariats pour promouvoir les droits, la sécurité et la dignité des femmes et des filles. Pour les organisateurs, mettre fin aux VBG nécessite une action collective et coordonnée des institutions, de la société civile et des communautés. Un appel à construire ensemble des communautés plus sûres et plus inclusives. items.title: Tinubu says credit guarantee scheme unlocked ₦46.95bn in first year
items.description: By Johnbosco Agbakwuru, Abuja President Bola Tinubu has said that the National Credit Guarantee Company has helped unlock ₦46.95 billion in loans in its first year of operations, part of the government’s drive to broaden access to formal credit for households and small businesses. The company, known as NCGC, issued ₦21.59 billion in loan guarantees that enabled participating lenders to provide financing to 67,512 borrowers in 25 states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT). President Tinubu disclosed this in a post on his official X account on Monday. The figures suggest that for every ₦1 in guarantees mobilised, about ₦2.17 in credit was drawn, illustrating the government’s effort to use public risk-sharing arrangements to draw more private-sector lending into the economy. obtain credit without comparable public support. Women accounted for 11,374 of the 67,512 borrowers reached, or roughly 16.8% of beneficiaries. The figure points to a continuing gender gap in access to formal finance, even as the credit-guarantee programme expands lending to borrowers who had previously been excluded from the banking system. The NCGC began operations in July 2025 and has used both individual facility guarantees and portfolio guarantees, the latter allowing lenders to extend credit to groups of smaller borrowers more efficiently. Its first-year results represent an early test of whether government-backed guarantees can materially expand private lending without the state becoming the direct financier of the economy. President Tinubu cast the programme as evidence that the government’s economic reforms are beginning to translate into opportunities for households and businesses. “We will keep widening that road until the opportunities our reforms create reach homes and businesses in every part of Nigeria,” he said. items.title: MRC/ Tournée nationale : Tiriane Balbine Noah verrouille le Nord et l’Adamaoua
items.description: © DR De Ngaoundéré à Garoua, la présidente nationale par intérim du MRC effectue depuis ce week-end une tournée nationale ouverte par le Grand Nord. La candidate à la tête du parti installe ses bases, présente son équipe pour la convention du 17 octobre et montre qu'après les démissions de Maurice Kamto et Mamadou Mota, le parti "reste debout". Huit heures de route cabossée entre les deux capitales régionales n'ont pas eu raison de sa détermination. C'est le message que veut faire passer Tiriane Balbine Noah au terme de son passage à Ngaoundéré et à Garoua.Vendredi dernier, c'est l'Adamaoua qui a ouvert le bal avec l'installation du bureau régional. "Merci à nos amis politiques de l'Adamaoua pour leur accueil chaleureux et leur mobilisation hier à Ngaoundéré", a-t-elle écrit après la cérémonie. Elle a salué particulièrement "les femmes, la jeunesse militante et l'ensemble des responsables et militants qui, chacun selon son degré d'implication, ont contribué à la réussite de cette belle cérémonie". Pour elle, cette mobilisation "témoigne de la vitalité de notre famille politique dans le Septentrion". Son mot d'ordre, lancé sur place : "Je reste à vos côtés!" Garoua : la démonstration de force Cap sur Garoua le lendemain de la cérémonie de Ngaoundéré. Autour de la secrétaire régionale Hadja Asmaou, la foule est conquise. Tiriane Noah y tient le discours le plus politique de sa tournée pour le moment. "Le MRC reste debout, vivant, uni et engagé, malgré les démissions de Maurice Kamto et Mamadou Mota. Nous allons continuer à promouvoir leur héritage à travers leur combat pour un Cameroun prospère et démocratique." Elle rappelle l'enjeu des législatives et municipales de 2027. D’après elle, cet enjeu est de prouver que le changement n'est pas un slogan. Dans la capitale régionale du Nord, elle dévoile aussi sa liste pour la convention nationale extraordinaire du 17 octobre 2026. Elle est accompagnée et soutenue par Mamadou Mota, ancien 1 er vice-président, coordonnateur général de sa campagne. Présent à ses côtés à Garoua, il tient un discours de mobilisation pour la continuité des activités du parti avec celle qui a toujours été là contre vents et marrées. A la suite de la tournée de Garoua, Mota publie un texte qui fait office d’adoubement officiel : "Le seul brevet d’aptitude qui vaille, en politique, n'est jamais celui du célèbre marketiste, encore moins du notable local enivré de sa propre notoriété. C’est le testament de celle qui a su tenir la barre et maintenir le cap alors que la tempête faisait rage..." Sans la nommer, il désigne Tiriane Noah comme celle qui a sauvé le navire MRC. Et il ajoute : "J’offrirai volontiers mon épaule pour guider la jeune garde". Il valide ainsi son rôle de parrain de la nouvelle génération. La bataille du 17 octobre est lancée La direction rappelle une règle cruciale pour la convention : seuls les militants encartés depuis au moins 3 ans et à jour de cotisations pourront voter. En 48h, de Ngaoundéré à Garoua, Tiriane Balbine Noah veut envoyer deux signaux : le Septentrion, souvent présenté comme difficile pour le MRC, est mobilisé. Et elle n'est pas une présidente par intérim par défaut, mais une candidate qui structure sa propre équipe, avec la bénédiction de l'ancien numéro 2. Ce lundi, elle boucle son périple dans le Septentrion par la région de l’Extrême-Nord avant de poursuivre dans d’autres régions. La tournée va s’achever la veille de la convention dans le Centre. Son adversaire du moment, Pierre Emmanuel Binyam a prévu de lancer sa campagne par le Littoral le 27 septembre. Sa tournée s’achèvera le 15 octobre, deux jours avant la convention. Cet article MRC/ Tournée nationale : Tiriane Balbine Noah verrouille le Nord et l'Adamaoua est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Membre non permanent du Conseil de sécurité de l’ONU : Le poids diplomatique d’un siège stratégique
items.description: Le président de la République, Bassirou Diomaye Faye a déclaré, jeudi passé, à New York, dans le cadre du débat général de la 81e session de l’Assemblée générale des Nations unies que le Sénégal allait présenter sa candidature à un à siège de membre non permanent du Conseil de sécurité pour la période 2032-2033. Un membre non permanent du Conseil de sécurité de l’Organisation des nations unies (ONU) dispose d’une influence réelle, mais différente de celle des cinq membres permanents (États-Unis, Russie, Chine, France et Royaume-Uni) qui bénéficient du droit de veto. Le Sénégal a déjà siégé à trois reprises au sein du Conseil de sécurité des Nations unies comme membre non permanent: 1968-1969, 1988-1989 et en 2016-2017, souligne le site de l’ONU. Une place au cœur des décisions internationales Le Conseil de sécurité compte 15 membres dont 5 permanents et 10 non permanents. Les membres non permanents sont élus par l’Assemblée générale pour deux ans. A la suite de leur élection, ils disposent chacun d’une voix. Pour l’adoption des décisions sur les questions de fond, le Conseil de sécurité doit réunir au moins neuf voix favorables sur les quinze membres, sans qu’aucun des cinq membres permanents n’y oppose son veto. L’abstention d’un membre permanent ne constitue pas un veto. Une résolution peut donc être adoptée avec une abstention d’un permanent, dès lors qu’elle obtient au moins neuf voix favorables, lit-on sur le site de l’ONU. Un membre non permanent peut par ailleurs faire recours à sa position, pour porter une question qui intéresse particulièrement sa région ou son continent. Par exemple, un pays africain peut chercher à faire davantage entendre au Conseil : le financement des opérations de paix, la lutte contre le terrorisme au Sahel entre autres. Un levier diplomatique impactant La présidence du Conseil de sécurité tourne chaque mois entre ses 15 membres, selon l’ordre alphabétique anglais des noms des pays. Lorsqu’un pays non permanent devient président, il acquiert pendant ce mois une visibilité et une influence supplémentaires. Il ne peut évidemment pas imposer seul une décision, mais bénéficie d’une capacité d’impulsion et de facilitation supérieure à celle d’un membre ordinaire. Un état membre non permanent peut aussi présider des comités de sanctions. Le Conseil dispose de nombreux comités et organes subsidiaires, notamment les comités chargés de différents régimes de sanctions. Des membres non permanents peuvent obtenir la présidence de certains de ces organes, précise la même source. La limite du veto Un membre non permanent ne peut pas bloquer seul une résolution substantielle. Les cinq permanents (États-Unis, Russie, Chine, France et Royaume-Uni) sont les seuls à disposer du droit de veto. En résumé, le siège non permanent ne donne pas de de veto, mais offre une place dans le centre des décisions internationales. La véritable force du mandat réside donc dans la capacité à influencer les textes, porter des dossiers, présider le Conseil, diriger certains travaux, négocier avec les P5 et faire entendre les priorités de sa région. Au vu de tout ce qu’il comporte, ce siège constitue une plateforme diplomatique de premier plan, offrant au pays élu une capacité accrue à défendre ses positions et à développer des convergences avec les autres membres du Conseil. Pour le Sénégal, un mandat de deux ans représente une opportunité de renforcer sa visibilité et son influence diplomatiques, notamment en portant les priorités du continent, sur les dossiers inscrits à l’agenda du Conseil. O.BA

items.title: Botola : une abondance de buts qui dessine les contours d’une saison offensive
items.description: La première journée de la Botola Pro D1 « Inwi » a esquissé les contours d'une nouvelle saison offensive au détriment des lignes défensives, les filets ayant tremblé à 27 reprises lors des sept rencontres disputées, dont 17 buts à l'actif des équipes visiteuses contre 10 pour les clubs hôtes. Ce bilan reflète une nette domination des visiteurs, qui ont remporté quatre victoires à l'extérieur, contre deux victoires à domicile et un seul match nul, en attendant le choc de la journée entre l'AS FAR et le Raja Casablanca. Le COD Meknès s'est illustré avec la meilleure performance offensive de cette journée inaugurale, en revenant du stade El Abdi d'El Jadida avec une large victoire sur le Difaâ par 6 buts à 2, lors de la confrontation la plus prolifique de la journée avec huit réalisations, permettant ainsi à l'équipe de la ville ismaïlienne de prendre provisoirement la tête du classement à la différence de buts. L'avantage des équipes visiteuses s'est étendu à l'Ittihad Tanger, qui a ramené une victoire par 3 buts à 1 de son déplacement contre le nouveau promu, Amal Tiznit, tandis que le Widad Témara a créé l'une des principales surprises de la journée en s'imposant face au cador le Wydad Casablanca sur le même score au Complexe sportif Mohammed V à Casablanca. Le Hassania Agadir a clôturé la série de victoires à l'extérieur en remportant un succès palpitant contre le Kawkab Marrakech sur le score de 3 buts à 2, lors d'un match marqué par cinq buts et permettant à la formation soussie d'engranger, à son tour, ses trois premiers points. L'Union Touarga a su exploiter l'avantage du terrain et du public pour remporter le derby de la capitale face au FUS sur le score de 2 buts à 1, alors que le Maghreb Fès a entamé la défense de son titre par une victoire sur la Renaissance Zemamra sur le même score. Le match nul et vierge entre le Moghreb Tétouan et la Renaissance Berkane a constitué l'unique exception d'une journée dominée par le rythme offensif, six des sept rencontres ayant enregistré au moins trois buts. Outre l'efficacité offensive, cette journée inaugurale a révélé des difficultés précoces au sein des lignes arrière de plusieurs clubs, le Difaâ El Jadida ayant encaissé six buts, tandis que les filets du Wydad Casablanca et de Amal Tiznit ont tremblé à trois reprises chacun, au même titre que le Kawkab Marrakech qui a concédé trois buts. Avec un bilan de six victoires et un seul match nul, cette première journée a permis à six clubs d’empocher trois points, avec à leur tête le COD Meknès grâce à la différence de buts, en attendant la clôture de la journée avec le Clasico très attendu entre l'AS FAR et le Raja Casablanca. Ce bilan riche en buts laisse présager une saison exceptionnelle dans ce domaine, tandis que les équipes promues ont confirmé leur capacité à rivaliser avec les clubs de l'élite. The post Botola : une abondance de buts qui dessine les contours d’une saison offensive appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Wife, daughter of drug lord Fito captured in Colombia
items.description: Colombian police have arrested the wife and daughter of one of Ecuador’s most powerful drug lords who was extradited to the United States last year, President Abelardo de la Espriella said Sunday. Adolfo Macias, alias “Fito,” is the leader of Los Choneros, a notorious Ecuadorian gang with ties to Mexico’s Sinaloa cartel. His wife Inda Mariela Penarrieta Tuarez and daughter Michelle Jamileth Macias Penarrieta, who are wanted in Ecuador for money laundering, were arrested in northeastern Colombia in an operation involving the FBI and Ecuadorian authorities, De la Espriella said. He said Ecuadorian authorities were investigating the women for “using shell companies to launder the organization’s (Los Choneros’) money.” “I will gladly send them to my good friend, President Daniel Noboa, so they can answer to Ecuadorian justice,” De la Espriella said in a post on X. “That’s how we work, Abelardo: together and with results,” his Ecuadorian counterpart replied on the same platform. Macias was captured and extradited to the US last year, after escaping from a prison in Ecuador’s port city of Guayaquil in 2024. He had been serving a 34-year sentence for involvement in organized crime, drug trafficking and murder. He faces seven charges in a New York court, including drug trafficking and arms trafficking, which carry sentences ranging from 20 years in prison to life. The US designated Los Choneros as a terrorist organization last year. Ecuador, once one of Latin America’s safest countries, has become a key cocaine transit hub between top producers Colombia and Peru, and consumers around the world. Mexican cartels have forged alliances with local gangs, including Los Choneros, who battle for the control of ports and shipping routes. items.title: 37e Traversée Dakar-Gorée : Ousseynou Diop règne, Aïcha Diop surprend
items.description: Ousseynou Diop (Asfa) a encore dompté la baie de Dakar. Ce 27 septembre 2026, le nageur des forces armées a remporté la Traversée Dakar-Gorée pour la cinquième fois d’affilée. Chez les dames, Aïcha Diop (Aoc) a créé la surprise en s’imposant devant sa coéquipière Fatou Sèye. Deux victoires signées Diop, lors d’une 37e édition marquée par une participation record de 1 024 nageurs. Cinq sur cinq. Ousseynou Diop ne lâche plus la Traversée Dakar-Gorée. Hier, le nageur de l’Association sportive des forces armées (Asfa) s’est offert un cinquième sacre consécutif, confirmant son statut de référence de l’eau libre au Sénégal. La victoire ne lui a pourtant pas été offerte. Parti à 12h23 de la plage de la Voile d’Or, sous une mer apaisée, il a longtemps nagé en tête avec ses coéquipiers Moussa Guèye et Adama Thiaw Ndir. Diop et Guèye ont distancé Thiaw Ndir juste avant le contournement, avant qu’Ousseynou Diop ne se détache avec autorité dans les dernières minutes. Chez les dames, la victoire a souri à une nageuse que peu attendaient. Aïcha Diop, de l’Atlantique olympique club (Aoc), s’est imposée au terme d’une course maîtrisée, devant sa coéquipière Fatou Sèye et Ngoné Diop, de l’Olympique de Ngor. Un doublé qui confirme la vitalité de l’Aoc et l’émergence d’une nouvelle génération de nageuses. Au-delà des vainqueurs, cette 37e édition restera celle de tous les records : 1 024 nageurs sur la ligne de départ, contre une vingtaine en 1985. « Il n’y avait pas seulement des nageurs licenciés : la moitié vient des plages. Nous avons eu des amateurs et des nageurs du corps diplomatique qui sont venus en masse. C’est donc une grande satisfaction pour nous », se réjouit Magatte Dièye, président de la Fédération sénégalaise de natation et de sauvetage. Le signal est fort : la Traversée n’est plus réservée aux initiés, elle est devenue une fête de la mer. Réunir autant de nageurs en pleine mer impose un dispositif de sécurité conséquent. Magatte Dièye a salué l’appui de la Marine nationale, du ministère de l’Environnement, du Port et, désormais, de la Police. Il retient surtout la forte présence des jeunes, à quelques semaines des JOJ Dakar 2026. « Il faut miser sur les jeunes. Les Joj vont peut-être servir de tremplin pour le sport sénégalais », estime-t-il. Reste à transformer cet engouement populaire en vocations, et ces vocations en performances. Par Marième Fatou DRAMÉ
